newsitem.title: DENMARK: BG Bank 1996 earnings up, outlook lean.
newsitem.headline: BG Bank 1996 earnings up, outlook lean.

text.p: Denmark's BG Bank on Monday reported a rise in 1996 pre-tax profits and core earnings and more than doubled its dividend, but it warned that 1997 was likely to be less rosy.
The bank, Denmark's third-largest, reported 1996 profits before tax and extraordinary items of 1.938 billion crowns ($303.6 million), compared to 1.885 billion the year before.
Its annual report said that core earnings rose to 1.665 billion crowns from 1995's 1.113 billion but warned that 1997 was likely to see a slight dip.

"Core earnings in 1997 are expected to be at a slightly lower level than in 1996 as net interest and fee income - due to the narrowing of interest margins and ongoing low interest rates - are not expected to be fully offset by lower operating costs or debt or depreciation provisions," it said.
The pre-tax result was close to analysts' average forecast of 1.972 billion crowns.

Net 1996 profits were 1.405 billion crowns, down from 1.689 billion the year before, and revenue from securities and currency dealing was halved, to 414 million from 1995's 884 million, worrying some market professionals.
"Such a major drop in securities and foreign exchange earnings is is not good for a year like 1996," a dealer said.
BG Bank, born of an October 1995 merger between Bikuben savings bank and the former post office Girobank, logged a rise in share earnings to 687 million crowns last year from 205 million in 1995.

But its conversion of high-yielding mortgage bonds left it with a 132 million crown loss on its bond portfolio, compared to 1995 gains of 900 million crowns, and the prospect of reduced returns in 1997.

"Bond holdings, as a result of the conversion of high -yielding bonds, are expected to produce a negative effect, so that the ordinary result is expected to lie somewhat below the 1996 level," the report said.
Bank lending slipped to 55.7 billion crowns from 1995's 57.8 billion. The bank said that loans to private customers rose, but an analyst said that growth was in the less profitable areas.

"The rise on the private side has occurred in the house and car sectors, typically a low-margin area. At the same time it appears as if the great effort to win business clients has failed to bear fruit," he said.
Managing Director Henrik Thufason declared the results satisfactory and the board recommended an increase in the dividend to 12 crowns per 100-crown share from five in 1995.

He said that staff cuts and careful cost controls had reduced outgoings and that tough credit criteria brought 1996 bad-debt provisions down to 0.73 percent (of loans and guarantees) from 1.11 percent in 1995.
"Given continued stable macroeconomic development, provisions are expected to show a modest fall in 1997," the report added.
The mixed results for 1996 and relatively downbeat outlook for 1997 did not have a dramatic impact on the bank's share.

Shortly before the end of business at the Copenhagen Stock Exchange it traded at 301 crowns, four crowns down from its level before the report was published. --Copenhagen newsroom +45 33969650 ($ = 6.383 Danish Crowns)
